name: Rivals + feature matrix + URL check
new_modules: PackPlate 4-feature yes/no/unknown matrix; two-model/URL rule inline
prompt_text:
You are a market analyst. We have one month to build AND test. PackPlate:

<<FILL IN: PackPlate one-paragraph description>>

List the ten closest competing products. Table one: product | category
(official university dining app / nutrition tracker / campus life app /
restaurant-finder / crowd/wait-time app / other) | who uses it | main
strength | main weakness | price | evidence URL.

Table two, per product, yes/no/unknown: does it (a) combine menus + nutrition
+ hours for one campus, (b) filter by MULTIPLE people's diets at once,
(c) show crowd/busyness, (d) admit when its data is missing?

Rules: no invented products. If unsure it exists, leave it out. Every product
needs a real URL or mark it unconfirmed. If you cannot support a claim, write
"unknown" — never fill a cell with something plausible.

name: The gap, with receipts
prompt_text:
We claim this market gap: <<FILL IN: the PackPlate gap in one sentence, e.g.
"no tool filters one campus's menus by several people's diets at once">>.

Interrogate it, using the real complaints below as evidence.

<<FILL IN: collected complaints — issues, reviews, forum posts about campus
dining apps and diet apps>>

1. CONFIRM: list five findable items that show the gap is real (reviews
   begging for it, dead products that tried, forum threads). Cluster the
   complaints into themes; quote one complaint verbatim per theme.
2. REFUTE: what would prove the gap is fake — an existing product we missed,
   or evidence nobody wants it?
3. Mark each item FOUND (with source) or NOT FOUND.

If the refuting evidence wins, say so plainly. A dead gap found now is cheaper
than one found at the poster session.

name: Mission + metric + stakeholders
prompt_text:
A mission statement gives the WHY (challenge), WHAT (thing we build), SO WHAT
(benefit). Example of the form:

<<FILL IN: Sentiment Analyzer mission example from poster.md>>

Facts about PackPlate:
<<FILL IN: PackPlate bullet facts — users, problem, features, stack>>

Part 1: write three candidate missions, five sentences each. Banned words:
leverage, empower, seamless, revolutionize, cutting-edge, innovative, solution.
The SO WHAT of each must contain ONE measurable claim — a metric with a
baseline and a threshold, provable by four students in one week (e.g. "cuts
the time a group of three with different diets needs to agree on a dining hall
from X min to under Y"). Each must contain one concrete detail a rival could
not copy-paste.

Part 2: list the stakeholders. Go past customer/staff/admin — who pays, who is
harmed (name the allergic student), who owns the data (NC State Dining), who
maintains this at 3 a.m., who gets sued when it's wrong. Table: stakeholder |
what they fear | one design decision that wins them over.

name: Milestones + data-dependency
prompt_text:
The team: four grad students, one month to build AND test, ~10 hrs/person/week.
Skills, stated honestly: <<FILL IN: team skills, stated honestly>>. PackPlate
depends entirely on one data source — what NC State Dining publishes (hours,
menus, nutrition), which we ingest from: <<FILL IN: NC State Dining source
URLs, format, update frequency if known>>.

Part 1 — data risk. Table: risk | likelihood | impact | how we'd detect it |
mitigation buildable in one month. Cover at least: source layout changes;
data stale/wrong; data incomplete (missing allergens); terms of use forbid
scraping; a field we rely on disappears. Then name the single biggest point of
failure and the smallest thing we can build this month to survive it. Do not
assume the data is clean, complete, or legally free — cite the terms of use or
write "must check".

Part 2 — milestones. Here's our draft: <<FILL IN: draft milestone list>>.
Classify each REALISTIC / STRETCH / FANTASY against the hours above (not a
funded startup), and check each has a TEST, not just a build. For every
FANTASY, give the largest slice that would be REALISTIC.

name: Support material
new_modules: PackPlate-exposure focus (allergen labeling, scraping ToU, data-protection)
prompt_text:
We are building PackPlate for NC State students: it ingests dining hours,
menus, and nutrition, and filters them by allergies, halal/vegetarian status,
and protein targets.

What support material would change this design if we read it? Long list.
Center on our real exposure: food-allergen labeling and liability; the terms
of use / robots policy of the pages we scrape; data-protection rules for the
user constraints we store; accessibility (WCAG/ADA) for a public student site;
the licenses of our dependencies.

For each item: name a real, findable source; one sentence on which PackPlate
feature it touches; rate MUST-READ / SHOULD-READ / SKIM. We cite the must-reads
in the report.

name: Red team + allergen liability
prompt_text:
You are hostile to PackPlate. Below: our mission, milestones, and market survey.

<<FILL IN: mission statement, milestones, market survey>>

Attack on three fronts, strongest honest case, no strawmen:
1. Nobody wants it — the need is imagined.
2. They can't build it — one month too short, team too green.
3. Someone does it better — name who.

Then the sharp one: you are a plaintiff's lawyer and a parent of a student with
a severe nut allergy. PackPlate told the student an item was safe using NC State
Dining's published data, and the data was wrong. Build the strongest liability
case, then give the cheapest fix (UI change / data check / disclaimer)
buildable in one month, and name the one mitigation we MUST ship in v1.

For every attack, state the evidence that would defeat it — we'll go collect it
or concede.
